title: The Golden Rule of Friendship
hook: A glove wrapper on an ambulance floor can teach more about liking than a perfect story about yourself.
counterintuition: Trying to impress often steals the very feeling that makes people return. The real move is to help them feel capable, seen, or useful.
tryThisNow: In your next conversation, ask one follow-up that makes the other person useful or understood, then leave your own matching story unsaid.
keyTakeaway: People warm to you when attention helps them feel better about themselves, as long as the attention stays sincere and does not become performance.

breakdown.fastRead:
The ambulance floor smells of antiseptic and rainwater while Luca studies a crumpled glove wrapper beside the run sheet. The new EMT is waiting for the verdict after a messy call.

Luca could show command by naming every mistake first. Instead, he names the exact patient-care decision the trainee handled well, then moves to the miss. The trainee straightens enough to hear the correction.

The Golden Rule of Friendship is simple: help people leave with a better sense of themselves. It is not flattery. It is attention placed where the other person can stand taller.
breakdown.deepRead:
Rachel points to a retired engineer's note on the library tech-help sign-up sheet. The magnifier lamp is still on, his volunteer lanyard still stiff from the drawer. "You caught what our form misses," she says, then asks whether he would help redesign the intake page.

The rule works when the good feeling belongs to them, not when your compliment calls attention to your own cleverness. The Golden Rule of Friendship says that if you want people to like you, make them feel good about themselves. The mechanism is emotional association: people tend to move back toward the person who left them feeling competent, respected, interesting, or understood.

Praise is cheap when it points back at the praiser.

That is why Rachel's sentence works. She does not call the retired engineer amazing. She does not perform gratitude until the room gets sticky. She names the useful thing he saw and gives him a role that respects it. He leaves with evidence of his value, not a ribbon made from someone else's charm.

The limit sits close by. If attention becomes a technique, people hear the gears. If making someone feel good means agreeing with nonsense, the respect is false. If you erase yourself completely, the exchange becomes service, not friendship.
breakdown.fullRead:
At 7:18 p.m., James watches a nervous beginner hold a figure-eight knot in chalky fingers at the edge of the top-rope lane. Her belay card is clipped backward. His chalk bag is open. He can fix everything in three seconds and look competent doing it.

Instead, James notices the one thing she did right. "You dressed the knot cleanly," he says, touching the rope below the loop. "Now let's turn the card so it matches your hand." He gives the correction after the competence has somewhere to land. The beginner does not have to survive humiliation before she learns.

What would change if you treated every correction as a chance to protect the other person's sense of worth? You would still correct. You would still say the hard thing. You would simply stop using your own expertise as the center of the scene.

The hard part is getting your own need to shine out of the center of the room. That ego override is more practical than noble. Ego loves to disguise itself as helpfulness. It wants the clever fix, the better story, the line that proves you know more. In a city planning meeting, Lukas can answer angry residents with a polished defense of the bus-lane map. Or he can repeat their concerns as practical local knowledge, point to the traffic maps curling at the corners, and ask where the map is blind. The second move does not surrender the proposal. It lets critics feel respected before they are asked to think.

This is the difference between flattery and outward attention. Flattery tries to purchase warmth with pleasant words. Outward attention gives the other person a more accurate experience of themselves. The new EMT handled one decision well. The engineer saw the flaw in the form. The beginner tied one part of the knot cleanly. The resident knows where the map fails at curb level. Those are not decorations. They are real footholds.

The rule can also be abused. A person can make others feel good only to keep control of the room. You can praise someone so they owe you warmth, validate them so they stop objecting, or ask questions that are really traps for your agenda. The moment the other person feels managed, the good feeling curdles. Sincerity is not an extra layer; it is the condition that keeps the move from becoming manipulation.

You do not have to disappear. Friendship is not built by becoming a mirror with no face. You can have your own view, your own standards, and your own correction. The move is narrower and stronger: let the other person's dignity arrive before your performance does. Make the good feeling about who they are or what they contributed, not about how smoothly you delivered the compliment.

People remember the room where they felt more capable. They remember who made that room possible. The memory follows the feeling, not the speech.

examples.title: Luca Finds the Good Decision First

planSpec.domain: a paramedic preceptor debriefing a new EMT after a messy call
planSpec.audience: a senior medic who wants confidence without false praise
planSpec.stakes: a shaky trainee may either learn or shut down
planSpec.requiredBeat: the preceptor names the exact patient-care decision the trainee handled well before discussing the miss, so the trainee feels competent enough to hear correction

examples.scenario: The ambulance floor smells faintly of antiseptic and rainwater while Luca picks up a glove wrapper beside the run sheet after a difficult downtown call. The new EMT is staring at the oxygen key like it might accuse him. Luca is about to start with the missed radio update, then stops. He must decide whether to lead with the exact patient-care decision the trainee handled well before naming the error that still needs work.
examples.whatToDo: Name the sound decision first, then correct the miss. Give the trainee one real foothold before asking him to absorb the harder feedback.
examples.whyItMatters: The trainee can hear correction better when his competence is visible. False praise would feel soft, but a precise strength gives him a stable place to learn from.

examples.title: Rachel Points to the Engineer's Note

planSpec.domain: a public library branch manager welcoming a retired engineer to a volunteer tech-help desk
planSpec.audience: a manager who needs the volunteer to feel useful without being patronized
planSpec.stakes: the volunteer may quit if treated like a mascot instead of skilled help
planSpec.requiredBeat: "You caught what our form misses," Rachel says, pointing to his note before asking for help redesigning the sign-up sheet

examples.scenario: "You caught what our form misses," Rachel says, pointing to a pencil note on the tech-help sign-up sheet. The retired engineer's library lanyard is still creased, and the magnifier lamp throws a circle over the desk. He shrugs like it was nothing. Rachel has to decide whether to thank him politely and move on or ask him to help redesign the sheet around the flaw he noticed.
examples.whatToDo: Treat the note as useful expertise. Ask for his help on the redesign instead of offering a vague welcome or patronizing praise.
examples.whyItMatters: The volunteer needs to feel skilled, not merely included. Naming the concrete contribution makes the good feeling belong to him.

examples.title: James Lets the Beginner Keep Her Knot

planSpec.domain: a climbing gym instructor handling a nervous adult beginner
planSpec.audience: an instructor who must keep attention on the beginner instead of performing expertise
planSpec.stakes: one humiliating moment could make the beginner leave the sport
planSpec.requiredBeat: At 7:18 p.m., James chooses to notice the beginner checking her knot correctly instead of showing off a harder move

examples.scenario: At 7:18 p.m., James sees a figure-eight knot held in chalky fingers beside the top-rope lane. The beginner's belay card is clipped backward, and his own chalk bag is open for a demonstration he does not need while two climbers wait behind her. James has to decide whether to show a cleaner advanced tie-in or notice that she checked the knot correctly before turning the card around.
examples.whatToDo: Name the correct check first, then fix the card. Keep the attention on what the beginner did well instead of displaying a harder move.
examples.whyItMatters: A nervous beginner can leave after one public embarrassment. Precise recognition lets correction feel like progress rather than proof she does not belong.

examples.title: Lukas Treats Anger as Local Knowledge

planSpec.domain: a city planning facilitator listening to residents angry about a bus-lane proposal
planSpec.audience: a facilitator whose credibility depends on making opponents feel heard
planSpec.stakes: a public meeting can turn hostile before the maps are discussed
planSpec.requiredBeat: the facilitator repeats the resident concerns as practical local knowledge and asks where the map is blind, making critics feel respected without surrendering the proposal

examples.scenario: Lukas stands beside a roll of traffic maps curling at the corners beneath name placards and a microphone stand. He hears residents describe delivery vans, school pickup, and the left turn everyone avoids after rain. He is about to defend the bus-lane proposal slide by slide, but he must choose whether to treat their anger as obstruction or repeat it as practical local knowledge and ask where the map is blind.
examples.whatToDo: Restate the concrete concerns as knowledge the map needs. Ask where the plan misses street-level reality before defending the proposal.
examples.whyItMatters: People soften when their experience becomes useful. Respecting the local knowledge lets them feel seen without requiring you to abandon the plan.

examples.title: Layla Names the Tradeoff Under the Bug

planSpec.domain: a software mentor reviewing a junior developer pull request
planSpec.audience: a mentor who must correct without stealing ownership
planSpec.stakes: the junior dev may learn the habit or start hiding mistakes
planSpec.requiredBeat: you can either showcase your own elegant fix or ask what tradeoff the junior developer was protecting, then name the sound instinct underneath it

examples.scenario: You see a red test failure beside a small green diff in Layla's 4:40 p.m. pull request review queue for a Toronto fintech sprint. Before, she rewrote junior code in a crisp review comment and watched the developer go quiet for two sprints. After, she asks what tradeoff he was protecting, then names the sound instinct under the bug before suggesting the fix. The code still changes, but ownership stays in the room.
examples.whatToDo: Ask what the junior developer was trying to protect, then name the useful instinct before the correction. Let the fix keep his agency intact.
examples.whyItMatters: A mentor who displays elegance can steal ownership. Recognizing the sound instinct makes the developer feel capable enough to keep learning in public.

examples.title: Juliette Starts With the Blend

planSpec.domain: a neighborhood choir director keeping an alto from quitting after missed entrances
planSpec.audience: a director balancing correction with belonging
planSpec.stakes: losing one singer will thin the section before a memorial concert
planSpec.requiredBeat: it takes two rehearsals for Juliette to realize the alto returns when feedback starts with the blend she adds, not the mistake she made

examples.scenario: It takes Juliette two rehearsals and a pencil mark beside measure 42 to see why the alto stopped meeting her eyes before the memorial concert. The sheet music is open on the folding riser, and a water bottle with a choir sticker leans against the leg. When Juliette begins with the blend the alto adds before naming the missed entrance, the singer returns the next week with the same folder under her arm.
examples.whatToDo: Begin with the real contribution the alto brings to the section, then correct the missed entrance in that context.
examples.whyItMatters: Belonging gives correction somewhere to land. If the singer hears only failure, the memorial concert loses her voice before the music improves.

questions.prompt: A mentor reviews a junior developer's pull request after a red test failure and wants the developer to keep learning in public. Which response best reflects the Golden Rule of Friendship?
choices: Praise the developer's effort in general terms
Name the useful tradeoff the developer was protecting, then correct the bug
Rewrite the code silently so the developer avoids embarrassment
questions.explanation: The second response makes the developer feel capable through a real observation. Generic praise is thin, and silent rewriting removes ownership.

questions.prompt: A senior medic debriefs a shaky trainee in the ambulance bay after a messy call and a missed radio update. Which opening best helps the trainee learn without shutting down?
choices: Start with the missed radio update so the trainee takes it seriously
Say everyone makes mistakes and move on
Name the correct patient-care decision, then discuss the missed radio update
questions.explanation: The correct patient-care decision gives the trainee a true competence anchor. Starting with the miss may trigger defense, and vague comfort avoids the lesson.

questions.prompt: A branch manager welcomes a retired engineer to a library tech desk. He quietly marks a flaw on the intake sheet. Which move best makes him feel useful?
choices: Ask him to help redesign the form around the flaw
Tell him the library is grateful for all volunteers
Explain that the form has always worked well enough
questions.explanation: Asking for help turns his observation into useful expertise. Vague gratitude is pleasant but weaker, and defending the form wastes his contribution.

questions.prompt: A climbing instructor sees a nervous beginner make one correct knot check and one equipment mistake. Which action best avoids making the moment about his own expertise?
choices: Demonstrate a harder knot to inspire confidence
Name the correct check first, then fix the equipment mistake
Ignore the mistake until she feels more comfortable
questions.explanation: The beginner keeps dignity while learning. A harder demo centers the instructor, and ignoring the mistake sacrifices safety for comfort.

questions.prompt: A city facilitator faces angry residents beside bus-lane maps, name placards, and a microphone stand. Which response makes opponents feel heard without surrendering the proposal?
choices: Repeat their local concerns as useful map data and ask where the plan is blind
Tell them the city has already studied the issue
Compliment their passion and move to the next agenda item
questions.explanation: Treating concerns as knowledge gives residents status in the discussion. Authority talk dismisses them, and complimenting passion dodges the substance.

questions.prompt: A colleague compliments everyone constantly, but people avoid long conversations with him because the praise feels like a performance. What is missing?
choices: Enough positive language
A stronger smile
Sincere attention tied to something real in the other person
questions.explanation: The issue is not praise volume. The good feeling has to be grounded in a real contribution or quality, or it feels like technique.

questions.prompt: A choir director begins feedback by naming the blend an alto adds before correcting a missed entrance. Why does that work better than starting with the mistake?
choices: It makes the correction optional
It places the correction inside belonging
It distracts the singer from the missed entrance
questions.explanation: The singer can hear correction while still feeling valuable to the section. The mistake is still corrected, and distraction is not the mechanism.

questions.prompt: A manager asks questions about an employee's weekend only so she can ask for overtime afterward. The employee leaves feeling handled. What failed?
choices: The manager chose a personal topic too early
The employee dislikes friendly managers
The attention served the manager's agenda more than the employee's dignity
questions.explanation: The surface question may sound warm, but the structure is self-serving. Outward attention fails when the person feels used as a route to compliance.

questions.prompt: A teammate made a costly scheduling error before a client deadline, and you need to correct it without turning the conversation into a status contest. Which plan best uses the rule?
choices: Open with three compliments so the teammate stays relaxed
Skip correction until the relationship feels stronger
Name the planning habit that helped, then address the exact error and next safeguard
questions.explanation: The plan protects competence while still correcting reality. Compliment padding feels artificial, and skipping the correction avoids the responsibility.

reviewCards.front: Someone leaves a conversation liking you more. What feeling probably increased?
reviewCards.back: They likely felt more competent, respected, useful, interesting, or understood. The good feeling was about their own worth, not about your performance.

reviewCards.front: You need to correct someone without shrinking them. What should come before the correction?
reviewCards.back: Name one real thing they did well or one useful instinct they showed. Then make the correction while their sense of competence is still intact.

reviewCards.front: A compliment feels fake even though the words are positive. What likely went wrong?
reviewCards.back: The praise was generic, self-serving, or disconnected from anything real. The rule needs sincere attention, not pleasant language sprayed over the room.

reviewCards.front: In a hostile public meeting, how can you make critics feel respected without surrendering your position?
reviewCards.back: Treat their concrete observations as useful knowledge. Repeat the specific concern, ask where your map is blind, then keep working the proposal from there.

reviewCards.front: Why does ego break the Golden Rule of Friendship?
reviewCards.back: Ego drags attention back to your cleverness, story, or status. The other person stops feeling seen and starts feeling used as an audience.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Move attention outward in a way the other person can feel. The skill is to name real competence, usefulness, or experience without turning the moment into your own performance.

ifThenPlans.plan: If I need to correct someone, then I will name one true competence signal before the correction.
If I feel the urge to tell a matching story, then I will ask one more question about the other person's experience first.
If someone criticizes my plan, then I will restate the concrete knowledge inside the criticism before defending my view.
If a junior person makes a mistake, then I will identify the useful instinct under the error before I explain the fix.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: In one conversation today, make the other person feel useful by asking for their judgment on a real detail, then resist adding your own story afterward.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: At the end of each day, write down one moment when you made someone feel more capable and one moment when ego pulled attention back to you.

memorableLines.text: Praise is cheap when it points back at the praiser.
memorableLines.why: It separates sincere attention from performance in a sharp line.

memorableLines.text: The hard part is getting your own need to shine out of the center of the room.
memorableLines.why: It names the ego problem in plain human terms.

memorableLines.text: People remember the room where they felt more capable.
memorableLines.why: It turns the social rule into an image readers can carry.
